sentences.speech: Build a complete Brick Breaker game in Scratch 3.
This self-guided course is for ages 10-14 with some Scratch experience.
Across six chapters, you will control a paddle, move one Ball, create 50 bricks that each take two hits, drop Apple power-ups, track three lives, and end the game when every brick is gone.
Use coordinates, loops, conditions, variables, costumes, clones, and broadcasts in Scratch 3.
Build a game loop that checks for a missed Ball before it bounces off the edges.
Make Ball the only sprite that checks for touching a brick, and use broadcast Hit Brick and wait so exactly one Brick clone reacts.
Create 50 bricks that always change from Healthy to Cracked before breaking.
Use Lives and Bricks Left to decide when the player loses or wins, and restart only with the green flag.
Test a multi-sprite project by checking one game rule at a time.
Know how to open Scratch 3 and start a new project.
Know how to drag blocks together and choose values from block menus.
Be able to rename sprites, costumes, backdrops, variables, and messages exactly as shown.
Use Scratch online at scratch.mit.edu, signed in to your Scratch account.
You will not download or upload project files.
Complete all six chapters in order.
Plan for 90-120 minutes per chapter.
Scratch saves your project to your account; also choose File > Save now at each chapter checkpoint.
To continue later, sign in, open My Stuff, and click See inside on your project.
Use the exact sprite, variable, costume, backdrop, and message names shown so your code matches the lesson.
Use the green flag as the only way to start or restart the game.
pixel
One of the tiny dots that make up the screen.
The Stage is 480 pixels wide and 360 pixels high.
coordinate
A number that says where a sprite is.
x goes from -240 on the left to 240 on the right.
y goes from -180 at the bottom to 180 at the top.
The middle of the Stage is x 0, y 0.
direction
The way a sprite points.
0 is up, 90 is right, -90 is left, and 180 is down.
variable
A named place that stores a value the project can change and check.
clone
A temporary copy of a sprite that uses the sprite's scripts but can move and act on its own.
one sprite, no clones
A sprite that never makes copies of itself.
Ball is one sprite with no clones, so "go to Ball" always means the same place.
collision
When two sprites touch.
broadcast-and-wait
A message that pauses the sender until every script started by that message has finished.
Hit Claimed
A shared variable that is 0 or 1.
Ball sets it to 0 before a hit.
The first Brick clone that reacts sets it to 1, so the other clones know the hit was already handled.
script that finishes
A script that reaches its last block because it has no forever loop.
broadcast and wait can only continue after every script it started has finished.
game loop
A repeating script that updates movement, collisions, and game rules many times each second.
state
The current condition of an object or game, such as Healthy, Cracked, playing, won, or lost.
Brick Breaker is easier to build when you separate what you see from the rules underneath it.
The player moves a Paddle.
One Ball travels continuously.
A grid contains 50 bricks.
Every brick survives its first hit by changing from Healthy to Cracked, then disappears on its second hit.
Missing the Paddle costs one of three lives.
The game is won only when Bricks Left reaches 0.
Watch the example once without trying to copy code.
Watch again and look for the Paddle, the one Ball, five rows of ten bricks, and falling Apples.
Notice that a first brick hit changes its appearance and a second hit removes it.
Notice that a miss removes a life instead of bouncing from the bottom edge.
Remember that the green flag is the only start and restart control in the project.
Count one row, then multiply ten bricks by five rows.
